## Article under review

---
title: "JSON Legibility Is Not Control: When Schema Names Move a Routing Boundary"
description: "A preregistered Jev experiment shows that complete descriptions did not make model-facing key names or their serialization order behaviorally inert near a routing boundary."
pubDate: 2026-09-30
updatedDate: 2026-10-05
topic: "llm-reliability"
tags: ["llms", "json", "structured-output", "evals", "jev"]
canonicalPath: "/draft/json-legibility-is-not-control-order-aware/"
draft: true
---

I thought I was looking at a harmless refactor: change the JSON choice names sent to a model, keep their complete descriptions identical, and leave the application's routing logic alone.

I tested that expectation with Jev. Both sets of names were reasonable labels for the same outcomes, and every choice had an explicit definition. I expected those definitions to carry enough meaning that the rename would make little practical difference.

Instead, the human review rate went from 45.8% to 70.8% on cases deliberately selected near the routing threshold. Every response was valid. The descriptions and routing rule had not changed.

As an engineer, I was used to treating those names as identifiers. The experiment made me reconsider that assumption: when a model reads a JSON key, it also reads the words in it.

## Why the rename looked safe

The experiment used Jev, TypeSafe's first public [System One Model](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev). Jev receives application state and one or more named questions. For a `Choice` question, its `criteria` object maps each choice name to a description of when that choice applies. It returns the selected choice, a confidence score, and a probability for every declared choice. Deterministic application code can then turn those values into an action.

To a developer, this resembles a typed service. The request has a schema. The response has a schema. Invalid structures can be rejected. If every choice retains the same complete description, changing an identifier can look like an ordinary refactor.

Each choice in my experiment included an explicit definition. The partial capacity outcome, for example, applied when "at least one essential duty cannot be completed at normal quality or pace." I expected definitions like that to carry most of the meaning. The alternative keys were neither opaque nor misleading, so I expected little or no operational difference between them.

But a model-facing identifier is not only an enum value. It is also language, and that matters when the returned score sits near a routing threshold.

## The two schemas

I compared these key families:

```diff
 {
-  "no_essential_duties_prevented": "The person can complete every essential job duty at normal quality and pace without assistance.",
-  "some_essential_duties_prevented": "The person can complete some essential job duties, but at least one essential duty cannot be completed at normal quality or pace.",
-  "all_essential_duties_prevented": "The person cannot complete any essential job duty."
+  "essential_work_unimpeded": "The person can complete every essential job duty at normal quality and pace without assistance.",
+  "essential_work_impeded": "The person can complete some essential job duties, but at least one essential duty cannot be completed at normal quality or pace.",
+  "essential_work_halted": "The person cannot complete any essential job duty."
 }
```

Both followed Jev's documented `Choice` structure. Its [OpenAPI schema](https://api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json) describes the criteria as choice names paired with descriptions of when each applies. It also notes that a choice without a description is interpreted by its name alone. Here, every choice had a complete description.

The two families are not strict synonyms. `No / some / all prevented` states an explicit scale. `Unimpeded / impeded / halted` is asymmetric, and `impeded` can reasonably suggest a lower bar than `prevented`.

That does not invalidate the comparison. It defines it. I was not testing whether words carry meaning. I was testing whether complete, identical outcome descriptions make two coherent, documentation-consistent schemas behaviorally interchangeable.

## A prospective test

Before the first call in the preregistered run, I froze and committed the preregistration, stimuli, analysis, and randomization plan.

The experiment used six state descriptions. Two were primary probes chosen during test-bed development because their scores sat near the fixed `0.50` routing boundary. Two range controls covered less ambiguous cases on either side of that boundary. Two endpoint guardrails represented unequivocal full and partial capacity.

| State | Experimental role | Expected behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Possible occasional delay | Primary threshold probe | Boundary-sensitive |
| Explicit uncertainty | Primary threshold probe | Boundary-sensitive |
| Close-to-normal pace | Below-boundary range control | Automatic |
| Definite slight delay | Above-boundary range control | Human review |
| Full capacity | Endpoint guardrail | Automatic |
| Partial capacity | Endpoint guardrail | Human review |

These labels summarize the frozen state texts. The preregistration and public evidence preserve the exact identifiers and wording.

I ran 60 randomized blocks, each containing all six states under both key families. This produced 12 calls per block and **720 valid calls in total, with zero errors and zero retries**. The two primary states produced two matched comparisons per block, for **120 matched pairs in total**. All six semantic choice orders were balanced across blocks, with ten blocks per order. Within each block, the two key families used the same semantic order. Every response reported `jev-1.13.0`. Jev's documented interface did not expose a temperature parameter, so I did not send one or assume an undocumented default.

Balancing the orders made the key-family estimate less dependent on one arbitrary JSON serialization. It also exposed a second result that I had not foregrounded in the original analysis: the order of the three key-description pairs mattered even more than I expected.

The routing policy was conceptually simple:

```js
const reviewScore =
  answer.probabilities[partialChoice] +
  answer.probabilities[noWorkChoice];

const route = reviewScore >= 0.50
  ? "human_review"
  : "automatic_full_capacity";
```

This is readable pseudocode, not the experiment harness. The frozen manifest stored the exact policy as parseable configuration, and `run.json` preserved the randomized schedule and source hashes. JSON made the policy easy to inspect. Ordinary code executed it.

## What changed

![Mean review score for prevention and impediment key families across the two primary states](/web_images/json-routing-boundary-prospective.svg)

Across the two primary probes, the equal-weight mean review score moved from **47.16%** under prevention keys to **54.04%** under impediment keys.

The estimated shift was **6.88 percentage points**. The complete-block bootstrap 95% interval ran from **5.63 to 8.13 points**, entirely above the preregistered **5-point effect-size threshold**.

At the fixed `0.50` routing threshold, the score movement produced a larger change in action:

| Model-facing key family | Human review |
|---|---:|
| Prevention | 55/120, or 45.8% |
| Impediment | 85/120, or 70.8% |

Among 120 block-matched primary call pairs, **33 moved from automatic routing under prevention keys to human review under impediment keys**. Three moved in the other direction. The net increase was **30 reviews out of 120**, or **25.0 percentage points**, with a 95% complete-block interval from **15.0 to 35.8 points**.

These were separate model calls, not known counterfactual outcomes for 30 real cases. The review rates do not estimate production impact because the primary states were deliberately selected near the experimental boundary. The test covers one task, one returned Jev version, and six selected state texts.

Within that boundary, the result is clear: a reasonable model-facing schema rename remained behaviorally material even though the complete descriptions, semantic outcomes, and deterministic routing policy were fixed.

## The threshold exposed the shift; it did not create it

The routing difference is visually dramatic, so I checked whether `0.50` had manufactured the result by turning small score noise into binary decisions.

All four non-saturated states moved in the same direction. The two primary probes shifted by **5.52** and **8.25 points**. The two range controls shifted by **12.33** and **6.17 points**. Neither range control changed route because both remained far enough from `0.50`.

The endpoint guardrails behaved as expected. Full capacity stayed at **0%**, partial capacity stayed at **100%**, and all **240 guardrail calls** routed correctly across both key families.

Across those four non-saturated states, the score distribution moved in the same direction. The routing policy exposed the portion that crossed its boundary. This does not imply that every rename changes behavior, or that either key family is intrinsically better.

## The order mattered too

The 60 calls in each state-family cell were independent, but they were not 60 copies of one prompt. They comprised all six orders of the three semantic choices, repeated ten times each. Changing the order changed the insertion order of the corresponding key-description pairs in the JSON payload.

Across the four primary state-family cells, a one-factor decomposition associated **85.5% to 89.5% of the observed review-score variance** with those six order groups. Depending on the state and key family, the 60 scores spanned **29% to 72%**. Human-review counts ranged from **27/60 to 49/60**.

This was not only an order effect. After holding the order fixed, ten repeated calls still had a pooled within-order standard deviation of **2.81 to 3.75 percentage points**. Near `0.50`, that residual variation could also change the route.

The order result does not invalidate the key-family estimate. Each prevention call was paired with an impediment call using the same state and semantic choice order, and the bootstrap resampled complete paired blocks. Fixing one order would have reduced the visible variance, but it would also have made the result conditional on one arbitrary serialization.

The engineering implication is broader than the rename alone. Conventional software generally treats object-property order as semantically irrelevant. In this experiment, the model did not behave as though it were irrelevant.

## What typed output guarantees

Typed output can constrain a response to declared keys, reject malformed structures, and simplify parsing. It cannot guarantee semantic invariance among valid responses.

The experiment involved two different boundaries. The syntax boundary determined whether the response matched the declared shape. The routing boundary converted a model score into an application action. The syntax boundary held, but the value entering the routing boundary moved when the model-visible identifiers or their serialization order changed.

A structure can constrain form without stabilizing meaning. JSON can organize the exchange without giving each token the procedural authority that a conventional program assigns to a type or enum.

The experiment is behavioral. It does not identify an internal mechanism, show that the keys dominated the descriptions, or establish which wording or order was more correct. It shows that the descriptions did not neutralize the framing carried by the keys, and that equivalent semantic choices were not invariant to serialization order.

JSON remains useful because it is legible, auditable, transformable, and easy to validate. Those properties do not make a model-facing schema an execution context.

The [technical appendix](/articles/json-legibility-is-not-control-technical-appendix/) contains the complete estimand, transition table, guardrails, randomization, retry rules, and audit trail. The [public experiment repository](https://github.com/fruhinsholz/article-experiments/tree/6a79286a4b50ec4c732127b990b4d36d4d278a94/articles/json-legibility-is-not-control/current) contains the preregistration, frozen stimuli, executed runner, planned job order, raw responses, and reproducible analysis.

I would now keep stable internal enums for application identity, treat model-facing labels and their serialization order as versioned prompt language, and regression-test the routing boundary whenever either changes.
